# Modeling Wire Train Bus communication using timed Colored Petri Nets

  * September 2008

DOI:10.1109/SICE.2008.4655160

## Abstract and Figures

Engineers in industry usually design new systems based on earlier experience and available development tools, Although this approach offers substantial advantages, there is also a great disadvantage. Introduction of new technologies is very difficult. Software modeling and simulation tools enable industrial users insight into systempsilas inner behavior before actually producing the system. In this paper a communication system based on the wire train bus is modeled using timed colored Petri nets. This system is verified for the desired properties and then it is validated. Validation is performed using two WTB units used in different real-life rail applications. The results, as well as possible future use of the model, are presented.

Abstract: Engineers in industry usually design new systems based on earlier experience and available development tools.

Although this approach offers substantial advantages, there is also a great disadvantage. Introduction of new technologies

is very difﬁcult. Software modeling and simulation tools enable industrial users insight into system’s inner behavior

before actually producing the system. In this paper a communication system based on the Wire Train Bus is modeled

using timed Colored Petri Nets. This system is veriﬁed for the desired properties and then it is validated. Validation is

performed using two WTB units used in different real-life rail applications. The results, as well as possible future use of

the model, are presented.

Keywords: Wire Train Bus, WTB, timed Colored Petri Net, CPN, modeling, validation, veriﬁcation, simulation

1. INTRODUCTION

Developing a complex system using only real-life

equipment could turn out to be an expensive undertak-

ing. Many engineer months are needed to purchase, in-

stall, program and connect all the necessary equipment.

If there are design errors detected during the test runs,

it will take many more engineer months to solve these

problems. Once the problems are solved, there are no

guaranties that all errors were detected and eliminated.

Development of a new distributed train control sys-

tem is now under way and the use of the Wire Train Bus

(WTB) as the communication protocol is considered by

the authors. The WTB is part of the IEC 61375 stan-

dard, also known as the Train Communication Network

(TCN), [1]. The TCN deﬁnes two types of communi-

cation busses: a vehicle bus, used to connect equipment

within a single vehicle; and a train bus, used to connect

multiple vehicles. The standard deﬁnes Multifunction

Vehicle Bus (MVB) as the vehicle bus, while WTB is

deﬁned as the train bus. In the development of the new

train, CANopen bus, which is based on Controller Area

Network (CAN) [2, 3], will be used as the vehicle bus.

CANopen has been recently submitted to the IEC to be

standardized as the rail-vehicle network 61375-3-3, [4].

Since software simulation tools for CAN exist, it is

possible to simulate CAN (and CANopen) communica-

tion network before any equipment is designed and/or

programmed. Such tools, for the WTB, are in develop-

ment, [5-7]. The authors decided to take a different ap-

proach, based on experience from [8], where a way to

model CAN communication using timed Colored Petri

Net (CPN) was described.

Having multiple communication protocols, i.e. CAN

and WTB, within the same development environment en-

ables simulation of even more complex communication

systems. Therefore, it is reasonable to model the WTB

protocol using timed CPN, too.

There exist both commercial and academic software

tools that can be used to simulate behavior of a CPN. Au-

thors use CPN Tools, a software tool developed by the

CPN Group at the University of Aarhus, Denmark [9, 10].

In order to verify and validate the WTB simulation

model, a simple WTB network setup was created in the

laboratory. The terms veriﬁcation and validation are ade-

quately deﬁned in [11].

The remaining of the paper is organized as follows. In

Section 2 a brief description of the development tools is

given. Colored Petri Nets are introduced and WTB net-

work setup is presented. Section 3 describes the CPN

model of the WTB communication network. The simula-

tion and experimental results are presented and described

in Section 4. The paper ends with conclusions and guide-

lines for future work in Section 5.

2. SOFTWARE AND HARDWARE

DEVELOPMENT TOOLS

2.1 Software tools and CPN

CPN Tools can simulate both basic Petri Nets and

more advanced Colored Petri Nets. The “color” or prop-

erties of the model are set using CPN Markup Language

(CPN ML), [12, 13]. Time is one of many properties that

can be set, so timed Colored Petri Nets are available.

Fig. 1 View of the CPN Tools with opened network

window and opened menus to create, simulate and

make state space analysis of the model.

Since CPN Tools simulate models using Petri Nets

there are only three basic elements. These are places,

transitions and arcs, Fig. 1. The “color” modiﬁes the

way a model functions. CPN Tools can create, simulate

and make state space analysis of the Petri Net model.

Basically, Petri Net is a directed graph composed of

two disjoint sets of nodes called places and transitions.

Places represent states of the system, while transitions

represent actions that the system can perform. To simu-

late an action performed by the system, appropriate tran-

sition has to “ﬁre”.

The “ﬁring” of a transition is enabled or disabled by

the tokens inside transition’s input place(s). If there is an

appropriate number of tokens in all input places, this de-

pends on connecting arcs’ inscriptions, then the transition

is enabled and it can ‘ﬁre”. The number of tokens created

in the output place(s) depends, again, on the connecting

arcs, Fig. 2, [14, 15].

2.2 Hardware tools and WTB

In order to verify the simulation results, two WTB

nodes are used. The laboratory equipment is set up as

in Fig. 3.

Fig. 3 The equipment used for WTB communication.

Using this equipment it is not possible to decode the

exact data in the frames, but, due to the network setup, the

frames were of different lengths. Since the WTB com-

munication is based on the master slave bus access, it is

possible to decode the “owner” of the data on the bus.

The WTB communication is a periodic master slave

communication protocol. The nodes are aware of their

place in the network, i.e. whether they are intermediate or

end nodes. The basic period of the WTB communication

is set at 25 ±1 ms. It means that every 25 ms the master

requests data from the slave, and only then does the slave

send the requested data.

The basic period is divided between a periodic phase

and a sporadic phase. Periodic phase occupies no more

then 60% (up to 15 ms) of the basic period, and is used

for “Process Data” exchange. The remaining part of the

basic period is occupied by the sporadic phase (min. 10

ms), which is used for “Message Data” and “Supervisory

Data” exchange. Periodic phase comes before sporadic

phase.

During the sporadic phase at least one “Supervisory

Data” exchange takes place. The master sends a “Pres-

ence Request” and receives a “Presence Response” mes-

sage. The master node sends the “Presence Request”

message every basic period to one of the end nodes (there

are always two end nodes). The master node alternates

between the end nodes every basic period, i.e. a node

receives a “Presence Request” every second basic period

(every 50 ms).

During the inauguration of the network, automatic net-

work setup before the actual data exchange, each slave

requests its own “Process Data” period. This period T is

deﬁned as T= 2 N∗25 ms, where N can have an inte-

ger value in the range [0,7]. In effect this gives a range

of periods, from 25 ms up to 3.2 s, for “Process Data”

exchange. All periods are multiples of the basic period.

All WTB frames have the same format, as given in

Fig. 4. The “Preamble” of the frame consists of 16 to 32

bits. Then an 8 bit opening “Flag” is sent. The 4 bytes

(8 bits each) marked as “DD”, “LC”, “SD” and “SZ” are

ﬁelds describing “Destination Device” (receiver), “Link

Control” (type of frame, e.g. “Process Data Request”),

“Source Device” (sender) and “Size” (number of use-

ful data bytes) respectively. Next ﬁeld contains useful

data. Number of useful bytes is deﬁned in “SZ”. It can

be in range [0,128]. A 16 bit “FCS” (“Frame Check Se-

quence”), as prescribed in ISO/IEC 13239, follows useful

data. Then an 8 bit closing “Flag”, identical to the open-

ing one, is sent. The frame ends with an “ED” ﬁeld, a 2

bit “End Delimiter”.

Preamble Flag DD LC SD SZ DATA FCS Flag E

Fig. 4 The WTB frame.

The bit stufﬁng prevents ﬂag sequence from appearing

in the data between the ﬂags. The transmitter inserts a “0”

after each group of 5 consecutive “1”s in the data. The

receiver removes the “0” which follows a group of ﬁve

“1”s. Stuffed bits are not visible in the data, but they may

increase the frame size up to 20%. In this paper bit stuff-

ing mechanism is used to make the distinction between

the frames from different nodes. Detailed description of

the frame formatting is given in [1].

The WTB network is set up as follows:

Node 1 - 24 bytes of data (all “1”s), 25 ms period;

Node 2 - 24 bytes of data (all “0”s), 25 ms period.

3. CPN MODEL OF THE WTB

COMMUNICATION NETWORK

In order to analyze the behavior of a complex system,

it is often useful to break down the system into smaller

components. Understanding the behavior of such com-

ponents and their interaction, enables understanding of

the whole system. The same approach is possible with

CPN using hierarchy.

In Fig. 5 a whole subsystem is replaced by a single

transition, so called substitution transition. This substitu-

tion transition hides the complex behavior from the ob-

server and enables easier understanding of the whole sys-

tem. If detailed understanding is needed, the observer can

look into the model of the substitution transition.

The CPN model of the WTB communication does not

include the inauguration process, as this would drastically

increase the complexity of the model, but would not in-

ﬂuence the behavior during normal runtime. Two nodes

were modeled, a master and a single slave device. The

WTB standard deﬁnes that the master of the network al-

ways gets node address (node ID) 1.

The slaves are addressed depending on their physical

location in respect to the master. If they are located “in

front” of the master they will be addressed as nodes 63,

62,..., 33. On the other hand, if the nodes are “behind” the

master, they will be addressed as nodes 2, 3,..., 32. The

IEC 61375 standard deﬁnes that up to 32 devices (includ-

ing the master) can be connected on the WTB.

In Fig. 6 two nodes are connected to the WTB. Nodes

are represented by substitution transitions Node 01 and

Node 02. Places Node2Bus,BusFree and Bus2Node are

used for the WTB data exchange between the nodes. Sub-

stitution transition WTB models the behavior of the Wire

Train Bus. Node 01 is the master while Node 02 is the

slave device.

The messages from the place TX RAM are sent to the

bus, place Bus2Node. This is only possible if the bus is

free. This state of the bus is represented by the BusFree

place. Once the message is sent to the bus, the transceiver

waits for the next action.

It can happen that the transceiver has to answer to the

message just sent, because the master polls itself for pro-

cess data just like it polls any other slave. If the master

polled a slave or itself, then it receives a reply message.

Once this message arrives the master sends the next mes-

sage. However, if the polling was unsuccessful, then the

master waits for the time-out to occur, and then it sends

the next message.

The WTB bus, shown as the substitution transition

WTB in Fig. 6, is given in Fig. 10. Messages received

from the nodes, via place Node2Bus, are processed. If

more than one message is sent at a time, then an error is

generated at the transition AddError. All nodes receive

the sent message via place Bus2Node. A log of all mes-

sages on the bus, for the comparison with real-life equip-

ment, is generated and stored in place Log.

4. SIMULATION AND EXPERIMENTAL

RESULTS

In order to verify and validate the simulation model

two tests are performed. The ﬁrst test is veriﬁcation of

the model using state space analysis capabilities provided

by the CPN Tools. The second test is validation of the

model. Simulation results from the CPN Tools are com-

pared to the results from the real-life equipment.

For the successful veriﬁcation of the model following

properties are required:

1. No deadlock in the system, i.e. system does not halt.

2. No error frames generated in the communication.

3. Existence of only one message on the WTB at the

time.

4. Existence of a message either in place Node2Bus or

Bus2Node at any given time.

For the model to pass the validation test following

properties are required:

1. Identical message order on the physical bus and the

model.

2. Same message duration on the physical bus and the

model.

4.1 Model veriﬁcation

The veriﬁcation of the model is performed using state

space queries within CPN Tools. In order to use state

space queries it is necessary to generate the complete

state space, i.e. to generate all possible states the model

can have. The model presented in this paper is of mod-

erate size and complexity, so it does not suffer from the

state space explosion, [16], but since time is one of the

parameters of the model it is clear that such a state space

would be unlimited.

Since the whole communication in the modeled sys-

tem is periodic, it is possible to generate a limited state

space. After some time, the communication pattern on

the WTB will simply repeat itself. Thus, by not observ-

ing the time parameter in the state space, a limited state

space can be generated. There is a surjection from the

whole state space to this limited one.

State space generation in the CPN Tools can be inﬂu-

enced by the branching conditions. A new state, called

node, is calculated from its preceding node. If there are

no restrictions on node creation, then all possible nodes

be created. However, if restrictions, i.e. conditions, are

included, then only some nodes will be calculated. For

the state space analysis used in this paper the following

branching condition has been used:

Nodes in the state space are compared to each other, but

without time marks. If there are two identical nodes with

different time marks, only one will be processed.

The state space of the model, generated without the

time parameter, has 452 states and 1148 possible transi-

tions. The model satisﬁes all four requirements. It has no

deadlocks, no errors are introduced, and only one mes-

sage at the time is present on the WTB.

5. CONCLUSION

The veriﬁcation and validation results presented in this

paper show that the simulation model can be used during

the development of new WTB based communication sys-

tems. The model will be used for performance analysis

of different WTB compositions.

Having both the CAN bus model and the WTB model

within the same development environment, it is possible

to simulate an even more complex system, e.g. two sepa-

rate CAN buses connected via two CAN-WTB gateways.

In order to obtain valid data from such models it will be

necessary to correctly model the inner workings of the

gateways, i.e. model the gateway’s software application.

Such complex systems will have to be created from

modular, composable parts, because state space analysis

for the veriﬁcation of the whole system will not be pos-

sible. Future work will also address a formal description

of necessary and sufﬁcient module boundary conditions

which could guarantee composability.

A model of the TTCAN (Time-triggered CAN) will

also be developed, because of the composability of such

a communication system.
